utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, tell me, please, how many of you were there on this meadow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't shoot at us on that meadow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were telling us how you were shot at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but not in the meadow that you're referring to. On the spot where I was, only they know how many people they killed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know how many of you were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know because there were two locations there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the one where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't count the men. I just know that in the hall, my assessment was that there were about 1.000 people. That's not the exact number. There may be more or less. According to our estimate, the way it looked in this gym, there were about a thousand of us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know how many people were taken out and shot at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the men were taken out. No one stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else save his life except you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, another three men survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell me how you saved yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came to execute us, they first opened a burst of fire from the right-hand side, and I fell because the men fell on top of me. My right hand remained across another man's chest who fell before me, and then an individual man came to shoot at the men one by one, and when the last shot was fired, I have a small scar here, probably a stone that ricochetted, and then later on other trucks arrived. They went further away from me. In the meantime, when night fell, the loader arrived, and the man who was driving the excavator, he was digging there, and this loader lit us all up. One man was alive close to me, but he was killed in the woods. The soldiers who were on duty there opened fire at that soldier. And then this man with the loader turned the lights around to light up the woods. I moved a little, and then he said, "We have another one here." However, they didn't shoot again. Then I crawled away towards this embankment, and I felt the rocks from the railway tracks. I looked around. No one was following. I got onto my feet, and I climbed up to the railway track. Someone opened fire. Whether it was in the air or somewhere, I don't know. Anyway, it was a burst of fire. I didn't feel any bullet hitting me, and then I ran into a maize field on the other side of the track. Then I went on my knees through the cornfield, and then I reached some bushes. I could feel the sound of water, but I didn't see any water. Then Serb soldiers came. They shot around in the cornfield, but they didn't hit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it possible that you weren't even wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I was just lucky. When I put my glasses on, I see this little scar and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they missed you. You were the only one they missed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just me. Another three men survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know those three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is their name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Redacted)was 20 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did all this last while you were there in this meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my estimate, more than half the night, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you go on to say that you returned to that spot. Why did you go back? You were fleeing. You just explained that you were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just fled to this other side of the same location. I didn't go back to the same spot. I came back there in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- just one moment. Yes, Mr. Waespi

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could briefly go to private session for one issue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 10 (Redacted) 11 (Redacted) 12 (Redacted) 13 (Redacted) 14 (Redacted) 15 (Redacted) 16 (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood yesterday, Mr. 1399, that you returned to that spot and that you saw in the moonlight corpses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is another location. When I escaped and reached the road, there's a stream next to the road, or some water flowing from a pipe, and that is the location where I saw those bodies. I didn't see bodies where I was because it was night-time. I could only see a little when the loader flashed its lights. I couldn't really see how many there were. There could have been a lot of them, because I went to that spot in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the fact that you went there in 1999 is another matter, but where did you see those other bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 200 or 300 metres away from that spot. There was one group one side of the tracks and another on the other side of the tracks. And there was no one there except for the dead bodies, no one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many bodies were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were a lot, because the killing went on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is that the same group that was with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement which you gave to the agency for investigation and documentation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the intelligence service, in other words, you said - at least that is what it says in your statement - that your eyes were tied, you were blindfolded, according to what you say, and that you recognised a certain Gojko Simic by his voice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is from the same area as you are.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the same municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. From the same municipality. And that you had worked with him in Belgrade in a building company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on what grounds can you claim that he is the one when you didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the man for some 15 years. I know his accent, and also they called each other by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard him call him by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they called each other by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify anyone else among those people except for Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know they called out Vojo, Risto, Gojko, and another one by nickname. I didn't know these two, so I can't say who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the shooting last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. It started around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, and it lasted until after midnight. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure about this man? They didn't call him out by first and last name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, but I can guarantee a hundred per cent that it was he. I knew the man, the way he spoke. And even if he was in another office and I would hear him, I would know who he was, not to mention right next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with a blindfold --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a blindfold then. I took it off. This may have been well into the night. However, it wasn't too visible because it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't really see that man, but you're claiming on the basis his voice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee 100 per cent that it is him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you guarantee that that is the man who perpetrated the crime, was this man found? Do you know anything about it? Did anyone call you in to testify about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he's alive or not. It's not up to me to look for him. It's up to other people to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, are you quite sure that things happened in the way you have described and that you can identify one of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me just this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have the English translation in sufficient copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to take a look at this, the 1st of August, 1995, and to see if his signature -- he thinks his signature is there and is it his statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.text: Very well. Now, Witness, I want to start off by asking you this, and it is something that you spoke about during previous testimony. Now, if you have the Serbian or, rather, B/C/S version of your statement of the 13th and 14th of August, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got the papers with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the occasion in that statement, it was a statement given to the investigators, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend, but we have to go into private session just for a brief moment again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the English version, it is to be found on page 6, paragraph three from the bottom. And the previous paragraph, the one before that.

utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's not waste too much time, please, on this. No, that's the B/C/S, thank you very much. Let the witness have the B/C/S, and we'll have the English. utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've already looked at that one. It was handed in a long time ago as the witness statement, in 1995. I do apologise, but I'm just dealing with documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We now have the statement made on the 13th of August, 1995, to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. That's it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we please take a look at page 6, paragraph three from the bottom. And I'd like to read it out to the witness. This is what it says: "Soon after that, 10 to 15 minutes later, I heard one more truck was arriving. I -- this went on throughout the afternoon and evening, and I heard that every ten or 15 minutes, one truck was arriving." You personally were shot at and that they missed. And you repeat that once more. So we agree there, do we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They shot at everyone, not only at me, but they missed me. Who said they just shot at me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They shot. Whether they shot at me or shot up in the air, I don't know because I didn't feel any bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said, "They shot at me and missed me." That's what you say here. Take a look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were shooting at me; they weren't shooting at you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't be angry with me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how wouldn't I be angry with you? If you're trying to escape and people are shooting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment now. Witness B-1399, we recognise of course that this is a very difficult and trying time for you, having to recall these incidents, but if you would be patient and just allow counsel to ask his questions and we will ask him to do so fairly rapidly because we need to move on. Yes. Perhaps we can move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to this topic, because I'd like to look at this particular subject given in a statement of the 1st of August, several days later after the event, and the statement given in 1997. And he says that they are his statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, would you please take a look at your first statement of the 1st of August, 1995, where you say that you spent two hours in that particular locality on the site you were shot, and then you said you moved to another place and spent three or four hours there. And I think the important thing for Their Honours is that neither in this statement or in the second statement in 1997 did you make any mention of the fact that you were shot at and especially, and this is the most important point, could you please explain to us why in these statements you don't mention the trucks arriving every ten minutes. So could you please explain that to us and Their Honours, why that is not contained in these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1399, what counsel is putting is that there are various matters which he's referred to which you haven't referred to in the statements. Assuming that that's right -- for the moment assuming that he's right, is there any particular reason why you didn't mention one detail or another? There may be a reason, there may not be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned all the details. Now, whether when both statements were printed out, written out, perhaps it didn't contain these details, but I did say that, that trucks came every ten minutes. And the fact that I moved the location was that I wanted to avoid the place where we were shot. And I spent a little more time in one place rather than another because they had killed all the people there. The shooting stopped, and then I went to save my own head. And this went on almost the whole night. I just had half an hour or an hour -- there was just half an hour or an hour before daybreak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more point. If I were to have time, there are more OTP documents here with respect to whether he recognised the site and location, and it would be interesting for you, but I don't want to go into that now because quite obviously I don't have the time to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the second statement and in a way in the first statement, too, you say the following -- look at the penultimate paragraph or, rather, the last page of your statement of 1997 and the one but last paragraph. utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you take a look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll give them the next C number, those three statements, I understand the last one to be translated. Perhaps the Prosecution would assist in making sure we get all the relevant exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is C20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B-1399, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. If you would just wait a moment while the blinds are put down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session again. Thank you.

utterances.text: We will have the next witness, please.

utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm assisted by Manoj Sachdeva in the presentation of this witness's evidence. utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your full name Francis Roy Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you by occupation a peace support training consultant and also a writer?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the early 1990s, were you a major in the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness's testimony has been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis (D). I will now present a summary of that evidence, and at one point, with your leave, I'll invite the witness to point out on the map alongside him the position of various places. By way of background, the witness was the United Nations senior military observer, known as SMO, in Sarajevo between mid-October 1993 and July 1994. He was a tank officer with 35 years experience in the Canadian army and had prior extensive experience with UN missions, in particular, peacekeeping missions. He has a Master's degree in war studies from the Royal Military College in Canada. The witness gave evidence to the following: That the UNMOs, UN military observers, monitored and reported events in Sarajevo. They were positioned on both sides of the confrontation lines around that city, and through a reporting system ultimately delivered to the witness as the senior military observer daily written accounts of their observations. This witness would then prepare a daily situation report known as a Sitrep each evening which was then distributed to sector Sarajevo, BH command, to Zagreb, and occasionally to UN headquarters in New York. During his tenure, there were up to 233 UNMOs under his command divided into six observation posts on each side of the confrontation line. Reference may be made to them as Lima or Papa posts. Lima as in Lukavica for the Bosnian Serb side. Papa as in Presidency for the Bosnian Presidency side. After the 5th of February, 1994, the Markale market incident, the structure of those teams was changed, at one stage peaking at 29 separate posts. They were positioned on the Papa side to provide observation of the city, incoming artillery and mortar rounds. They were not necessarily in the best positions to observe outgoing Bosnian army, ABiH, artillery and mortar fire. A number of these Sitreps generated during the witness's tenure reporting Bosnian Serb sniping and shelling activity against the city were tendered and they are exhibit numbers 5 to 10 and 15 to 24 on the exhibit list. The witness gave evidence that three of them were misdated as December, the month of December, and should have been January 1994, and they are exhibits 15, 19, and 20. In those Sitreps, certain terms are used: "Random fire," which the witness defined as referring to no distinguishable target; "harassing fire," which he defined as fire being used, for example, at a water point to make people that go to get water inconvenienced. They are either going to have to take shelter, there may be some casualties, but it is only harassing in the sense that you do not call down a major concentration of fire. Randomness was also a factor in harassing fire. Some of these tendered Sitreps refer to the shelling of Kosevo hospital by Bosnian Serb forces. The witness explained that when he received such reports he took steps to determine whether the Bosnians had used the hospital grounds for screening outgoing mortar fire, and although this practice was never confirmed by any UNMOs during his tenure, he suspected that that sometimes happened. He recollected that occasionally the Bosnian Serb army deliberately targeted with artillery the covered and protected routes used by civilian pedestrians to traverse the city, avoiding lines of sight from Bosnian Serb snipers. And by that artillery fire, they caused significantly higher casualties than usual. That document is P2088. He identified an UNPROFOR report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Now, we don't want to get these documents muddled up. We need in this trial to refer to our documents, and the way we do it in this trial is we don't have any P numbers, we have a number. So we are operating in Exhibit 585, and so there's no confusion, we then have the various tabs in 585.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. That's tab 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness identified in his evidence an UNPROFOR report in relation to an incident on the 24th of January, 1994, when six children were killed by mortar fire. That report concluded that the source of fire was the Serb side in the Stup or Ilidza area. He identified another report - that was tab 12 - an UNPROFOR report in relation to an incident on the 4th of February, 1994, in Dobrinja, and I note that is the day before the Markale market incident, when a number of adults and children were killed by mortar fire. That report concluded that the direction of fire was from the Lukavica area on the Bosnian Serb side. And that is -- I'm sorry, the earlier report is tab 13 and this is tab 12. In relation to the extent of civilian casualties, the witness gave evidence that the UNMOs made nightly visits to the morgue on the Bosnian Presidency side in order to confirm the number of casualties, number of deceased. They were not given the same opportunity for confirmation by the Bosnian Serb side. In December 1993, the witness commenced keeping a separate summary of casualty figures from shelling and sniping, and after the 5th of February, 1994, the Markale incident date, he stopped keeping this summary in relation to shelling since shelling temporarily stopped. So all figures after that date relate to sniping. Between March and June 1994, he compiled a summary of sniping casualties figures identifying civilians, and that status was determined by UNMOs on the following basis: The females were considered to be civilians since it was rare for women to be in the Bosnian military. Children, of course, were civilians. And military-aged men, unless clearly civilian, for instance by their occupation, were considered to be non-civilians. In respect of protests made by the UNMOs as to shelling or sniping, they were made through the Bosnian Serb liaison officer, Major Indic. When firing did stop following these protests, it was not possible to tell whether the UN intervention had been instrumental. If firing continued, that would be reported up the chain of command and the UN force commander or deputy would then send a formal note. UNPROFOR would also send formal notes of protest. Following the Markale incident, there was an agreement in February 1994 which resulted in an informal cease-fire. Prior to that time, from the arrival of Major Thomas in Sarajevo in mid-October 1993, the shelling had generally been into the city. The UNPROFOR commander, General Rose, announced in February 1994 that he expected at noon the following day that both sides would stop firing and if anyone shot after that, the media would know which side was not adhering to the cease-fire. The witness said that the agreement was a missed opportunity because the soldiers on the ground on both sides seemed to want it to hold but it was not respected. Between then and July 1994 when he departed, there was no artillery fire into the city, but the sniping resumed on the 1st of March, 1994 and was increasing in intensity when he left. The ABiH, that's the Bosnian Presidency army, took advantage of the cease-fire to improve their positions which was a source of -- subject of complaints by the Bosnian Serbs. Based on reports that the witness received from his subordinate UNMOs, the witness was able to identify certain locations as being regular sources of Bosnian Serb sniper fire. These included a church tower in a field opposite Lukavica from where Dobrinja was targeted. I now invite the witness to indicate that position on the map.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the School of Theology in Nedzarici, could you please indicate that approximate position as well.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The site in Grbavica opposite one of the UNMO observation posts.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, a geographical feature known as Sharpstone or Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the record, I should indicate that the map is Exhibit 343, tab 7. In relation to Sharpstone, the witness was able to visit that area and witnessed a very well dug-in position, "And there was no need for any special facilities for the snipers. They could just pick a trench and prepare themselves to shoot and then move to another trench and have a very clear view." He said there were a significant number of casualties from snipers located at that point. He said that poor visibility, such as from fog or other climatic conditions, affected sniper fire since they tried to use their weapons at their maximum range from about one kilometre. However, visibility was not so important in relation to indirect fire weapons since they relied on target identification by forward observers. In relation to the degree of command and control exercised by Bosnian Serb army commanders, he characterised the system as being similar to that of a NATO army in a general sense. Most of the brigade commanders were ex-JNA officers who were quite professional with operational and tactical skills whereas most of their soldiers had come from the Territorial Defence, or TO. He noted that given the extended period following the February cease-fire agreement with no Bosnian Serb artillery or mortar fire being launched into the city, that it followed to his mind that the Bosnian Serb army leadership exercised firm command and control over their subordinates who surrounded the city. In respect of sniping activity, he concluded that was controlled at the brigade or battalion level. For example, the Bosnian Serbs would explain that they engaged in sniping activity because the Bosnians were digging tunnels or trenches. That was one example. The UN would then negotiate an agreement that the Serbs would stop shooting if the Bosnians would stop digging. On occasion, the leadership of two opposing battalions would agree to a cease-fire and their soldiers appeared to genuinely desire one, but the sniping would continue, indicating the orders to snipe came from a level higher than the battalion. In terms of sniper control within a battalion, he said that sometimes there would be instances of sniper fire which appeared to him to be done with no reference to the overall corps situation. He noted that both parties acquired Motorola radios which had been stolen from the United Nations. They used those to listen in on UN communications which made available to them information as to shelling and sniping incidents. The witness said that in relation to fire into the city, that if the intention was to destroy Bosnian army command posts, it did not make much sense since he expected that the Bosnian Serb leadership would have had the necessary intelligence to know their precise positions and they had sufficient weaponry to destroy them. The witness also said that most of the Bosnian Presidency army brigades had fixed areas of defence which roughly correlated with pre-war defence plans under the old Yugoslavia. In relation to clothing, he noted that many people, including women and children, wore camouflage, where -- and many who were military wore civilian clothes, and this was explicable in part by foreign aid often involving camouflage clothing. That concludes the summary. I have no further questions to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start with my questions, let me just clear up, because it says on my statement Francis Thomas Roy, according to which I would conclude that your surname is Roy. Am I right or wrong? What is your surname, please?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: My surname is Thomas, and my second name is Roy and my first name is Francis, but most people know me by my second name, Roy Thomas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just asking that to know how to address you, Mr. Thomas. I didn't want to call you by your name or your nickname, so I wasn't quite sure as to which is which. So everything is all right now. Mr. Thomas, in your position as senior military observer, which means head of all the 200-odd military observers, you were in that position for eight months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No, actually nine months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nine. Your predecessors, Kukkola from Finland, was only there for four months, and a Swede for only two months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the period during which you held that position, that is for all of nine months that you spent there, I assume that your experience is much greater than that of the others who had much shorter tours of duty there in that position. Is that a logical statement, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, as briefly as possible, give us reasons as to why these two gentlemen spent such a short time in that position. Why were the changes so frequent?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That would be a decision made by the chief military observer in Zagreb. I really can't explain why he made these decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Military observers under your command, as has been stated, were two teams, Lima and Papa, and of course the teams for the safe areas of Gorazde, Zepa, et cetera; isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I was also responsible for Gorazde and Zepa, but not Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I only mentioned Gorazde and Zepa. The main duties of military observers as members of these Papa and Lima teams were to monitor exchanges of fire between the parties to the conflict, to establish the number of casualties, to monitor activities on the front lines, to maintain contact and links with the brigades, delivery of humanitarian aid, et cetera. Would those be the main duties?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you compiled reports about all your observations, which were known as Sitreps that the representative of the other side mentioned a moment ago; is that right? The situation reports, as they're known.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these reports written on a daily basis, that is every day, and forwarded to the head of the military observers?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, on page 4 of your statement, paragraph 7, you say that this was being done with a view for both Zagreb and New York to have a more realistic approach to the events than the one offered by the media. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume you were very well familiar with the media reports, and you commented on them on the basis of your direct insight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No, only when there was -- I was asked to or direct contradictions of my reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could you assess in the simplest terms to what extent and in what way the media reports differed from the reports you obtained through your military observers.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The media had less coverage on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would be the main difference, would it? And as an example of a disproportionate and different reports on -- of the same event, on page 5, paragraph 1, you refer to the situation in Sarajevo on the 20th of December, 1993. Is that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I'd have to look at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will remind you. Is it true that the Muslim side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will draw your attention to the passage that I would like you to comment on. You say, "The Bosnian side established that there were hundreds of killed and wounded. After verifying in medical institutions and morgues, it was established that in fact only 17 had been killed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were saying that you did not rely on hearsay but actual physical counting, and you "took special pride in the meaning 'UNMO confirmed."' I assume you found the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's on page 4 of the statement. I can see the witness looking for it. 2643 is the top number. The large paragraph near the foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just reading the Serbian version, and the pagination doesn't agree. So I assume you've found it now.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. If you could repeat the initial question, then I can answer it at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, actually, that an example of the discrepancy and difference between media reports and your own objective reporting is the example that I referred to. The question is: Is it true that the Muslim side reported that hundreds had been killed and wounded, whereas on the basis of checks it was established that only 17 people had been killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: In this particular case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, you say that you were proud of your reports because they relied on physical evidence and not on hearsay.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, can you give us an example of the Serbian side representing untruthfully or without objectivity an event that you yourself reported on?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I could probably, looking carefully through my Sitreps, give an example where we made a protest about a shelling incident in which case it might have been denied, for example, by Major Indic, that any shelling took place at all. There were many occasions where we protested something and which Major Indic indicated it couldn't possibly have taken place, when we made the first protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that you would check out what actually happened after that.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct. And normally if we reported shelling, then the shelling did take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that same passage, you say that you found with regret that the Serbs did not register their losses as the Muslim side did because they did not wish their casualties to be known, as you say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume that nevertheless, during those nine months you were able to learn that the losses on the Serb side were quite considerable too.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we were never given access to the morgues on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the addendum you say, among other things - but we'll come back to that, it refers to Markale - you say that you didn't have access to the Serb side comparable to the access you had on the Muslim side. Was the reason for this that the Serb side believed that the information collected by your observers could easily be leaked to the enemy side? Was that their conviction?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No. I think that was their excuse for denying us access when we wanted it, because in those areas where we were allowed freedom of access, I don't think that they could claim that information they -- that we obtained was in fact used by the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you say that the Serb side didn't want their casualties to be known, as you yourself say, tell me, as an officer with a great deal of experience, and especially in UN peacekeeping operations, do you believe that there is greater damage to the truth done by false reporting? We've just referred to one example when there was reports of hundreds, whereas in fact there was 17. Or is more damage done when there are no reports, as you were unable to receive any reports from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a totally hypothetical question which I cannot see that the witness can answer. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6, in the sixth paragraph you say that the Serbs around Sarajevo applied the policy of holding on to positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As someone who, in addition to the military aspect also is interested in history and other aspects, when talking about these Serb-held positions, as you say there are policy was one of holding, when we're talking about these Serb positions, were they captured positions or were they positions in areas mostly inhabited by the Serbs before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I'm not completely aware of how much was inhabited by the Serbs before the conflict started as my understanding was the city was intermixed ethnically, so there were areas of Serbs living inside Sarajevo and Bosnian people that lived outside. So I couldn't say what was the situation before the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will give you an ethnic map of Sarajevo based on an official census in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and as you spent all of nine months there, you know very well to interpret this map. It's both in Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we are -- if we're going on to a separate matter such as this map, we'll do so after the adjournment. Major Thomas, could I remind you, as we have to remind all witnesses, not to speak to anybody, including the Prosecution, about your evidence until it's over. Thank you. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the legal officer would come up, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's on now. I provided the usher with the map to show Major Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Thomas, could you just briefly answer this question: The positions where the Serbs were, were they mostly the positions where they lived or were they won over positions? In general terms, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it's too difficult for me to answer that, because when I arrived, I do know that there were Serb people living in the area that was held by the Bosnians. I also know that one neighbourhood, Grbavica, was in particular a Serb area, but there was three areas - Stup, Nedzarici, and the outskirts of Dobrinja - which I know there were people of different origins living there. So I think that if this -- if the accused's question was related directly to Grbavica, the answer would be yes, the Serbs in Grbavica were defending their own terrain. And the other areas of the city, I'm not so sure. And that's the best answer I can give on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Thomas. Thank you for that. I should like to draw your attention to that same paragraph in which you say that the Serbs around Sarajevo followed the policy of holding positions, and you say here: "I did not see the Serbs launch a single attack." That's the second sentence -- "I did not witness any Serb attacks." That is the sentence in that short paragraph. So throughout the time you occupied the post you did, you did not witness any Serb attacks. Isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I did not witness any Serb attacks in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6, paragraph 5, you go on to say that in October 1993, you noticed a very well-equipped Muslim force and group trying to take control of the Pale road, the Serb connection between Pale and Lukavica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what group of Muslim forces was it in actual fact, what kind? Perhaps you could use military terminology. Establishment-wise, I mean, what was it like?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: These were infantry ground troops using hand-held weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume they were members of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right? Because it was located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that these forces, as you yourself say, were very well-equipped, and they had French equipment? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: There's some confusion with that statement. The troops I observed with French equipment was observed in January 1994. The troops involved in the attacks that I observed in October 1993, I wasn't close enough to observe their actual equipment; I could only observe the firing and shooting and movement of the people in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say January 1994. I'm just looking at the addendum, the addition I was given yesterday, and you speak of another event. Seventy Bosnian soldiers wearing French helmets and flak jackets and so on in the offensive operation at Grbavica. Now, you yourself -- in fact, what you say here is in the third person singular: "He asserted that the men were from the Bosnian army after he stopped and asked them."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I personally saw these soldiers, I personally talked to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That means that until you stopped to talk to them, you weren't able to ascertain whether they were members of the BH army because they were dressed like French soldiers, is that it?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: They were wearing French-style helmets and French-style flak jackets. I should add for the benefit of the Judges that it was about 11:00 at night, dark, in January 1994, with no lights. So basically I'm looking at the silhouettes of soldiers crossing the road with helmets and flak jackets as the only real indicator as to what nationality they would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first idea that came to your head, as far as I can understand it from your explanation, was that they gave the impression of being French soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from this, may we deduce that by wearing what they were wearing they were in fact camouflaging themselves and could lead the enemy to make a false conclusion, and the enemy might think that they were members of UNPROFOR in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers that I knew manning the trenches in Grbavica I doubt would make that mistake. Travelling by myself in a UN military vehicle and just catching a glimpse of people jumping across the road is one thing, but to have people crossing the front line directly in front of you from military terms is another thing, and I do not think that people that have been in the front line for the length of time the Serbs had been in Grbavica they would have made that mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in view of the assertions you make that Sarajevo was totally blocked, in view of the position you held as the principal UN military observer, can you give us an explanation as to the way in which these Muslim forces came by the French equipment? Which channels did they use?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I have no idea on this. It was a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume that we're not challenging that the weapons and military equipment throughout the conflict, in addition to the total blockade and international embargo enforced on the export of weapons, that nonetheless, this equipment did reach the Muslim forces in Sarajevo through certain channels. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can only say that there were a large number of criminal elements at work on both sides and that weapons could be purchased from anybody, including Serbs, if you had the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but these weapons, without a doubt, were of French origin. So it's difficult to imagine that it could have been bought from anyone. Isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I would not say -- I would say that soldiers in any army may have sold their personal equipment for money if offered enough money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does that mean that the French sold their equipment for sufficient sums of money to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if the price was right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I would say that there was certainly no official French government agreement to sell any arms. I would say that individual soldiers from -- and some of these soldiers may have been from the Foreign Legion, may have sold their equipment. It may not have even been French soldiers that sold this equipment. Soldiers from armies collect equipment from other countries as well, especially equipment they think is better than their own. If I could have bought a French flak jacket, I would have bought one because it was better than the Canadian one that was issued me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on page 7, paragraph 4, you say that the commanders of the brigades on the Serb side had more confidence in drawing up local peace agreements, as opposed to the Muslims who, as you say, were little more conscious of hierarchy. Is that what you said? "Whereas the commanders on the Bosnian side seem much more conscious of their hierarchy."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that with the military representatives of the army of Republika Srpska you found it easier to reach agreements on cease-fire, peace agreements, as you call them, and that the directives for drawing up agreements when it came from the Muslim side just came from one place?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: What it means is that if a cease-fire was agreed with by a local commander on the Serb side, that he -- that that agreement would be adhered to. On the other hand, even if a Bosnian local commander made an agreement, it might mean nothing if it didn't have the approval of the higher commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Mr. Thomas, now, tell me, please, how frequently did the Muslim side open mortar fire on Serb positions using the military UN observers and observer posts as protection? Do you have any evidence of that during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, but I wouldn't characterise it as frequent use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume that the Serb artillery on such occasions responded to the attacks and tried to neutralise the sources from which the mortar attacks came.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs could be counted on to retaliate no matter where the fire originated from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you sometimes see them targeting any UN positions?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: What I can specifically say is that one of my OPs was fired on by an indirect fire weapon because the Serb artillery was trying to engage a mortar that was within a hundred metres of our position. And as you know, the danger area for mortar fire is more than a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this kind of conduct and starting an attack from close up, the kind you witnessed, was being used and resorted to by the Muslim forces vis-a-vis your OPs, did it threaten the safety of your people? It did, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, but if the Serbs had given us time to get the Bosnian forces to move, or given us more time, I think perhaps the retaliatory fire which threatened our people would not have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they didn't put your men in jeopardy despite all that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No, they certainly did. When they fired at a Bosnian mortar that was close to my OP, Papa 2 to be precise -- correction, Papa 3 to be precise, we didn't have time to ask the Bosnians to move the mortar before the first rounds were coming in, and they were all within an area -- within the area of the OP sufficient that I had to tell those people to go to their shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 9, paragraph 4, you state and I quote: "The Bosnians were prone to using heavy artillery and shot with the aim of causing a fire, such as shooting from the hospital compound or placing a mortar on a wagon or transferring it to the PTT building." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the PTT building, for instance, the United Nations had its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that by opening fire from the hospital that also puts the hospital in jeopardy because the place at which fire is opened is a legitimate military target for the opposing side in the conflict; isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Only if you accept that one wrong justifies another wrong. It's wrong to fire at a hospital. It's also wrong to use a hospital grounds as a baseplate for a mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what the Muslim forces did; right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The Bosnian forces, which we were never able to catch them doing, we suspected used hospital grounds to fire mortars, but we know for sure, because we observed the fall of shot of Serbian artillery on the hospital grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell me this, please: What you say, are they correct on paragraph 5 of page 9? You say that, "The greatest advantage of the Bosnian Serbs, the great supremacy in tanks and artillery, was not of great advantage to them in the fighting that took place in the urban sections. Their use of artillery and tanks to shell Sarajevo in an attempt to affect the will of the Bosnian government in fact had little impact."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through the shelling and as the international media were placed around the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, they tended to report the war based on the situation in the city; isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you consider that it was precisely because of these reasons that the Muslims opened fire in Sarajevo on those positions?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: If I understand your question, you mean you consider it precisely because of those reasons that the Bosnians opened fire from those positions. Is this my understanding of the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, from those positions.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. The answer to that question is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace -- just a second. Can I have the witness statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about sniper activity, Mr. Thomas, on page 8, paragraph 5, you state that from the Muslim side they were strictly controlled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who controlled them and guided them?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The minister of interior controlled the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The minister of interior controlled the snipers that I observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your contacts with the Serb side, did you hear their complaints with respect to sniper fire coming from the Muslim side and the great damage that it incurred in the lives of people on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Not as often as we should have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Mr. Thomas, that the Muslim sniper positions existed even in the government building, for instance, where the government had its seat?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it true that the media, when it came to sniper activities in Sarajevo, created an impression with the world -- with world public opinion - how shall I put this? - gave out an unbalanced picture of the actions taken by the two sides?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: In my opinion, the world media did give an unbalanced picture, but the reports provided by military observer organisation and other UN agencies provided a balanced view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was that balanced view? Could you state in general terms what the balance of forces was between the sniper activity of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Snipers were used as an instrument to get people to deviate from the agreed upon cease-fire. Both sides used sniper activity to try to influence the other side. The example that I used in my report, the testimony you're referring to, was of where a cease-fire was broken by the Serb side because three pregnant Serb women had been shot by snipers, and then the troops in the line, of course, fired the next day at every Bosnian soldier they saw on the front lines. That particular item was never covered by world media. It still doesn't change the fact that the cease-fire was broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you've precisely said, Mr. Thomas, that the Muslim snipers killed three pregnant Serb women, and the Serbs retaliated and responded by shooting at the soldiers on the Muslim side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, but of course the soldiers they shot were not in any way involved in the sniper activity. As I clearly stated before, snipers were controlled by the Ministry of Interior, which was not even the army, so the soldiers in the front line had no control over who and when used sniper fire on their side, on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume that minister of the interior was a Bosnian minister of the interior; right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it true that sniper activity from the Serb side was very often caused by fear of infantry attacks from the Muslim side? And you say something about that in paragraph 4 of page 8.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. Sniper fire was used to persuade the Bosnians on the other side of the trench lines to not do any further work to improve their trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Thomas, did both sides consider all men to be soldiers regardless of whether they were actually wearing uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can only assume they did. I assumed that all men were potentially soldiers because I couldn't tell whether they were soldiers or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that many members of the armed forces in Sarajevo on the Muslim side were not in fact wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: There was a blockade which stopped them from getting uniforms from anywhere, and there weren't enough inside the city to equip them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were not wearing uniforms and yet they were soldiers. Isn't that right, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct. There was more on the Bosnian side wearing partial uniforms than there were on the Serb side. But then I must remind you that Lukavica was a former army depot where there was probably no doubt a great quantity of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is beyond dispute. In connection with this question of uniforms, your statement on page 8, paragraph 7, is correct, isn't it, that if we're talking about men as targets of snipers, one could not talk about merciless killing of civilians, in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. If the target was a man, he could have military potential. If, obviously, he was able to carry a weapon and he wasn't too old. Unfortunately, many of the targets weren't men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslim side used sniping to initiate fire from the other side out of revenge?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Major Thomas, that by the end of 1993, from the Muslim side within the territory of Sarajevo a large number of armed units were active that were headed by local criminals?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Actually, in November, as my testimony given earlier mentioned, there was an attempt by the Bosnian government to get rid of the criminals that were in charge of formed military units, and I think I refer to that in that witness statement that you are also using. And that was November 1993. So by the end of 1993, I think they were actually getting rid of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have at least a general idea as to the number of Serbs in Sarajevo who were victims of the horrific crimes made -- committed by these units that I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No. If there was criminal activity, I think it was directed against the general population at large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention now, Major Thomas, to the second paragraph on page 10, when you say: "In the course of October and November, I saw moves by the Bosnian side to clean up the criminal element within the city," et cetera. That's what you said a moment ago. "The Bosnian side hijacked a number of UN vehicles including an APC. On the 19th of October, 1993, Bosnian soldiers disguised as Serbs shot at," it says here, "the BH commander. The Bosnians also began to use tanks firing from within the city in what I thought was an attempt to draw retaliatory fire." So they were disguised as Serbs and they shot at whom?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: They shot at the UN UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina. And yes, that statement's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't doubt at all the correctness of that statement, but what do you assume could have led to Bosnian soldiers disguised as Serbs to shoot at the UN commander of the protective forces for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I would make the logical assumption that they wanted to try to put the blame on the Bosnian Serb forces, but unfortunately, they weren't clever enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean fortunately.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in December 1993, the Muslim forces burnt to the ground all Serb houses in several villages around Han Pijesak? You speak about that on page 10, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that all Serbs, regardless of sex and age, who were in those villages, were killed on that occasion during those attacks?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Major Thomas, that such attacks went on continuously from October until the end of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That I can't confirm. I only did one investigation, and I was never asked by the Bosnian Serbs to do any further investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in those attacks a series of Serb villages were destroyed and the Serb inhabitants in them?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: This information I obtained by -- on my own initiative from asking different people about what could have happened over the period October/November, but I repeat again, I was never asked by the Bosnian Serbs to do any further investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Thomas, that is to your honour that without any request from the Serb side you collected information and sought to obtain an objective picture. So therefore, on the basis of what you did collect, though this was not required of you by the Serbs, did you gather information which pointed to the destruction of a series of Serb villages and the Serb population in that period?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can't confirm it. I would only say that there were indications that there was a use of this technique to influence the Bosnian Serbs' local population, but this cannot be confirmed by investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to learn which Muslim units carried out such attacks?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Major Thomas, on page 12, paragraph 4, you speak about the Serb attacks on Gorazde; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 11. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that on the 25th of March, you left Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 25th of March, you visited Gorazde. Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I brought two military observers there and two doctors for UNHCR. It also gave me an opportunity to visit my team there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that about that time there were organised attacks by Muslim forces from Gorazde on surrounding Serb villages and positions?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can't confirm it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that in connection with the events in Gorazde and the environs, from the 7th to the 9th of April you attended meetings at the Sarajevo airport chaired by General Rose, and the participants were General Mladic and Delic, that is the commanders of the Serb and the Muslim sides?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that those negotiations were also attended by an American envoy?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I don't remember the American.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mention him because I found some information about this in General Rose's book. So as -- I won't ask you about that as you don't seem to remember. And is it true that at those meetings held from the 7th to the 9th of April the Serb side advocated a cessation of hostilities throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not just in Gorazde and the environs?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslim side did not accept the proposal for hostilities to cease?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: They did not want the cease-fire line fixed for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were their reasons, in your conviction, Major Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: As I stated in my witness statement, the Bosnians did not want a country-wide cease-fire, lest the front lines become cemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they told at those meetings by General Rose that a cease-fire creates the possibility for all other matters to be dealt with by negotiation, that that was a necessary precondition for the problem to be resolved peacefully, for the killing to end?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I'm sure that's one of the arguments that General Rose put forward, but since you've read his book, you probably know more about it than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Thomas, despite the endeavours of General Mladic to have a country-wide cease-fire, and despite the fact that that proposal was rejected by the Muslim side, shortly after that, air attacks came against positions of the army of Republika Srpska though it was advocating peace throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The air attacks were in response to continued Bosnian Serb attacks on the so-called safe haven of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it quite certain that they had suggested a cease-fire not only in Gorazde but throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb position at the meeting at Sarajevo airport clearly emphasised that without a cease-fire throughout Bosnia, there would be no cease-fire at Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your side - and when I say "your side," I mean the United Nations - and the main representative in those talks, that is General Michael Rose, did advocate a country-wide cease-fire, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. The UN position has always been that the fewer people killed, the better the peace will be. And as long as fighting continues anywhere, people will be killed. However -- however, the Serb attacks continued in Gorazde while the talks were undergoing -- were under way in the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the negotiations were not successful, as far as I can gather, but you're an eyewitness, you can either confirm or deny this, because the Muslim side did not accept a cease-fire. Is that right, Major Thomas?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can only say -- I can't add anything that you haven't already read in General Rose's book. He was the chief negotiator for the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Major Thomas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at tab 28, first of all, in the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise to Mr. Kay and to Major Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Namely this piece of paper that I received subsequently is something I just forgot about, though I did refer to it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Thomas, on this one-page document, it says the source is Thomas Roy Francis, Markale 1. This is a document given to me yesterday. It has no ERN though. It is an information report. I assume you have a copy. I should just like you to comment on what you say here. You say that -- it's better for me to read it in English. "The witness said that within two days after the incident of the 5th of February 1994 at Markale marketplace, [in English] he and his patrol went out in the direction of fire, being north-east of the market. Witness observed backed up -- backed up 120-millimetres mortar on wheels within the confrontation lines on the territory of the Bosnian government forces. Witness stated that it was observed in a place where it could have fired at the marketplace. This was possible. However, witness states that in the two weeks immediately preceding the Markale marketplace incident, he and other UNMOs had been repeatedly denied access to the Bosnian Serbs held territory on the direction of fire, although they were given access after the incident." [Interpretation] Would you be kind enough, please, to tell us to the best of your knowledge, Mr. Thomas, what is your conviction as to who was behind this incident at Markale marketplace on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: There have been two or three UN reports, including one that was tabled as -- as evidence at the Galic trial, an initial report submitted by the French, so I don't think I can add anything. I wasn't privy to further investigations. Those -- those UN reports are available, and I can't add anything to those reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about your opinion, not about the reports. What is your best recollection of what happened? You were there.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He may be, but it may not be a matter which is really within his competence to deal with. If it is, of course, Major Thomas, deal with it, if you have a professional opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My professional opinion is it can't be determined who fired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us say that your professional opinion is correct, so it is not possible to establish who fired it, but there was a general hysteria against the Serbs who were immediately blamed of having fired it. Isn't that right, Major Thomas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this is going beyond the witness's competence. We've heard evidence about this from other people. The witness can deal with his professional opinion, of course, and he's given it. Now, let's move on. Mr. Kay. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just dealing with a couple of other matters from that statement that you made in that statement of the 10th of November of this year, Major Thomas.
