Casualties figures in the UN Sitrep reports, casualty figures from artillery including mortar fire made no distinction between military and civilian victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do say that in relation to sniping, casualty records recorded civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is that insofar as you believed them to be civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's using the criteria that's already been established by the Prosecution. Men of military age looking capable of fighting were considered to be military -- possible military soldiers. Women and children were excluded from the -- as being possible military people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Let's turn now to tab 28. This is a document with which you're familiar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Could you confirm that this is exactly the same as the document he's holding? Because his looks much thicker than mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that because I've got it along with other papers, and in fact the one you're looking at has three pages, whereas our tab 28 I've discovered only has two pages; is that right? You've got three pages there on this Description of Warring Factions is the first page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just going through this document with you, it was compiled as an assessment of the two sides, is that right, Bosnian troops being the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Bosnian Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in it you say: "The Bosnian troops have been re-organising since the spring of 1993."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I should clarify. This was a briefing prepared for me when I took over as senior military observer in Sector Sarajevo. So this was prepared by the people who were preparing me to assume command of that position. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 28893 to 28905.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was their status report of that time. That would be the correct way to describe it?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. It was their status report when I took charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what they were telling you was that the Bosnian troops had been re-organising in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was at the time that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, of course, was being debated between the two sides - I'll use that phrase - is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, although I wasn't in Yugoslavia in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The estimate, if we look at the middle of the page, was that the Bosnians had approximately 25.000 men in arms in Sarajevo, of which one-third were permanently on the front line.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no because this was prepared for me as my start point by other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can comment, though, on whether your team was inaccurate, incompetent or whatever, because it's part of your documents that have been produced through you, you see, by the Prosecution. So --

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. I accepted that as my start point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your start point was 25.000 men in the Bosnian -- Republic of Bosnia army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of the commanders having poor control of their units. And if we turn to the next page, command had been given to presumably a general you knew, Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ex-JNA, lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The summary of the report is that there was a shortage of JNA experience within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were JNA-trained officers?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps without the benefit of the very good Yugoslav War College.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You give on this second page -- or they gave to you, if I put it that way, an assessment of the forces being about 1.000 men on Mount Igman and the system by which they rotated men and the composition of the forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was presumably so that you as the incoming officer would be aware of what you were facing up to?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a comment in the middle of the page in that section on Mount Igman that it is remarkable that the defensive positions are also facing towards Hrasnica. Can you explain that to me. Just above the section on Serbian forces around Sarajevo. Middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: To me, one military posture is to have all-round defence and perhaps they thought that Hrasnica was vulnerable and could be penetrated. This would be depending on the Bosnian commander, how vulnerable he felt his rear area would be. And that was an indicator to me that perhaps they felt that Hrasnica was not very secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hrasnica being the place as well there was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Hrasnica was at the base of mount Igman and it was the territory held by the Bosnians on the far side of the airfield, so it was more than just a question of a hospital, it was a question of key strategic ground which permitted access to Mount Igman and then the route over Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And that was also where the site was of a hospital?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that hospital?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to give an assessment of the Serbian forces, a great deal of which you've already told us about, that they had a specialist -- more heavy weapons within the area, which we've heard about already. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. You've heard my indication already that the Bosnian Serb forces had more artillery and tanks and armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a page missing off this document in this tab here, but you've got another version of it, haven't you, with your papers -- with your statement that you made on the 10th of November, 2003, the one that you were looking at earlier, a last page with a separate assessment of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No, I don't have that with my tab either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that, you'll be able to deal with the question, I'm sure. The rest of the document went on to say: "It is very unlikely that the Serbs tried to take over the whole of Sarajevo by force."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was the military assessment of the time as to what was happening in the war between the two factions.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. And it also goes along with my own assessment which I said the Bosnian Serbs were in a holding position around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The heavy weapons were being used against the city, but they didn't have the manpower or the manpower was not in place there to move in and take over the city.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct, and any military officer would tell you that it takes more manpower to seize control of an urban area than it does open ground and that tanks are much less use in urban areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you were looking at here, in fact, through your period was a conflict between the two sides which was in fact not being conducted in a way of total warfare, i.e., to take the strategic objective of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I think that the -- well, the answer would be -- I'm not sure there was a strategic objective. I think there was a campaign plan for Bosnia, and I think that Sarajevo was -- was intended to be held by the Serbs, and the Bosnians had a reservoir of manpower there which they would try to make use of to influence the campaign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we turn now to tab 13 within the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could a copy of the exhibits be put before the witness so he can follow. Thank you. The first few pages of tab 13 are in the original French report. If we just turn to the page in English. And this concerns the 22nd of January, 1994. Your Honours will remember when Mr. Ierace introduced this document, he referred to tab 4. That was in fact an error. It's tab 13 that relates to the 22nd of January, rather than tab 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This concerned a strike being launched from a zone under the control of the -- probably launched from a zone under the control of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was no more definite than that, and at the end of the page, "Conclusions of the MIO. Bearing in mind the previous analysis, the strikes could have been launched from the Stup area, the Serb part of Ilidza"?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No more definite than that. Let's just go to tab 34 now. This deals with an issue that's already been raised with you in part by Mr. Milosevic but it's helpful to see it on the document as well. Tab 34, Exhibit D119 in another case, and it concerns six UNPROFOR soldiers and two armoured personnel carriers went to rescue observers who had been captured by soldiers of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and they were then later freed but some of the UN equipment was kept behind, an APC and other equipment, armoured personnel carrier. Can you see that at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This incident against the UN by people described as the Bosnian Herzegovina soldiers was commanded by a local Bosnia-Herzegovina leader called Kako. The status of Kako is what I'm interested in. Would it be right to say that he was a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: He was one of the -- that brigade, in fact, the 10th Mountain Brigade was the brigade that was acted against by the Bosnian forces in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a paramilitary until that moment?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I would not say so. It depends how you would consider the Bosnian forces in the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you then was what was the status of this unit here that was taking on the UN equipment and the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: They were considered to be members, to the best of my recollection, of 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So part of the official Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. And as you -- as I later advised, that brigade was dissolved, and it's in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This theft of UN military equipment was quite a regular occurrence, it seems, through your situation reports that you have.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: No. This was the only case that I know of of an armoured personnel carrier being taken by anybody during my nine months, and that armoured personnel carrier was returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the radios that were stolen?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Radios was a different matter. They were very portable, and I should tell you from other UN experience, the same thing happens -- it happened to me in Haiti. Not to me personally, but it's a question of Motorolas, which are a very desirable item, and people wanting to hear what the UN was doing made them a very attractive item, and it's very easy to steal them. It's a lot harder to steal an armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't know, but the French uniforms could have been stolen from the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: There were no free uniforms there and the soldiers weren't stripped so we know they kept their uniforms. Their personal belongings were taken, and this what lends the element of criminality to it. For example, the observers lost all their money that they had in their kit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: So -- but most of the equipment was returned except for things, and you'd have to ask a French officer involved about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have no need to go into that in any detail. What I was asking arose from the information within these reports of theft of military equipment and it was something, in my view, that needed being clarified.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Is that clarified enough?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we just look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Judge Kwon has a copy of this, I believe, is the only copy on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We all have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm under five minutes. I'm just dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 9 in the English version, and you were asked questions by Mr. Milosevic, about the third from bottom paragraph in mid-December 1993 --

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- investigation of attacks by Bosnian soldiers on several Serb villages near Han Pijesak. There is a further matter also within this paragraph, which was this: "I learned from an intelligence source, aerial surveillance --" I don't know want to know about that confidential information, but it -- "showed that from October 1993 onwards there was a pattern of villages destroyed in the same manner."

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That is an assessment based on the information available to me, which I can't say much more about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't want to know any of the sources of it or what it's about, but merely this, that material was being produced before you to show that this had been a pattern of conduct in the area committed by those forces against Bosnian Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Well, the problem with aerial surveillance is it only indicates that these villages were destroyed. There is no evidence to determine exactly who did it. And this is why an investigation on the ground is required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The investigation only took you to those several villages near Han Pijesak. After that, it was closed down.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I was only asked to investigate one village, and there is a UN report on that particular investigation that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed a copy was provided. Page 10. Near the foot of the page, fourth line from the bottom, during the brokering of the ceasefire agreement, this is post the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, when you in your role, I suppose, was trying to implement the cease-fires between the two sides. Would that be a correct generalisation?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: This was -- it wasn't -- this is General Rose's February 1994 cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes. I would be doing my best to implement the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You were being used, with the others, to try and then bring in the elements that would make it work.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bosnians wouldn't allow any weapons to be collected on Mount Igman, as proposed by the UN, and UNPROFOR didn't force the issue.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the Serb side, Pale was exempt from the agreement.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I need ask about on that. And an overall assessment can be put in this way as well: There was provocation on both sides breaching the cease-fire by the use of snipers to incur a retaliatory reaction against the other side.

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Thomas, you said that in your professional opinion it wasn't possible to determine who fired the mortar shell that was responsible for the Markale market incident, and you mentioned that there were some UN reports or investigations at the time, a French report. Did you understand that an analysis was carried out of the crater impact created by that mortar shell at the time?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you understand that that analysis yielded a direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other sources of information that were accessed by those carrying out the investigation other than the crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: They asked sources -- anybody that could have possibly heard outgoing mortar rounds. They asked the agencies that could provide patrol assets to determine if there was any firing units in the pattern or the cone to see if these units were there or could have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it transpired that they were witnesses or persons at least along the line of fire that had made observations or heard the sound of the mortar being fired, would that potentially, in your professional opinion, have allowed a conclusive report to be generated?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Based on what was reported to me, no. There was not evidence. We didn't have the evidence to establish who fired it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any persons having claimed to have heard the mortar being fired as reported by any of those investigations at the time?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. I mean, I don't know the result. I only have access to one of the reports, and there was a very thorough investigation done by the United Nations which again redid the crater analysis, which again went into great depth on this matter, and I think maybe perhaps the Court's already heard from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the personnel who were involved in that particular investigation?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: As far as I know, the major study of the first market massacre was led by Colonel Gauthier of the Canadian Forces, a field engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, elsewhere in your evidence this morning you made this observation: "I did not witness any Serb attacks in the Sarajevo area." When you said that, what type of attacks did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I had the simple military one that people went forward to the front lines to try and take a position held by the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could that perhaps be accurately paraphrased as gaining territory?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: In the case of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were also cross-examined on the topic of the shelling of the area of the Kosevo hospital, and you said that, "We observed the fall of shot of Serbian artillery on the hospital grounds." In relation to those observations, did any of those observed shots impact with hospital buildings?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to whether there were any civilian casualties caused by Bosnian Serb fire landing in the vicinity of Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: I can't recall at this time. There perhaps were, and it would require me to go through all the Sitreps to pick out. We would have noted it in a Sitrep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there are such references in the Sitreps generated during the time that you were the senior military observer, would that indicate that there were such casualties?

utterances.speaker: Francis Roy Thomas
utterances.text: Normally we would have put it in if there had been casualties in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will exhibit the statement, since it's been referred to fairly extensively, and we will mark -- I think we'll mark for identification now, Mr. Ierace, this ethnic map. It's been going backwards and forwards, we might as well mark it for identification. We will mark the map with the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it will marked --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- marked for identification. And it's perhaps simplest to give the statement, the witness statement the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D216 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There is no need for that to be marked for identification, that one is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Thomas, thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now over. You're free to go. I think it would be sensible to adjourn now. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thirty seconds in private session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibits to be tendered for the next witness include two maps. I'm not sure whether you wish them to be part of Exhibit 343 or exhibits to be dealt with in the normal way, with separate tabs for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think they might as well be part of this exhibit which we have here since it's dealing with a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you think the statement that was exhibited should go in with this witness's bundle as well? Because it would be easier to track that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Major Thomas's statement became a D number, but it occurred to me when I was dealing with it that it might be better off in the main file and then we can track it with those tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's think about that. I don't propose to decide that at the moment, but we'll make a note to consider it. Now, we'll have the next witness, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Mirsad Kucanin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the early 1990s were you a police officer working in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honours, in a similar fashion to the last witness, this witness's testimony in the Galic trial has also been tendered and I seek to present a summary of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it a number first, that and the entire bundle. The next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is 586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll seek to abbreviate the reading out of the summary. Mirsad Kucanin was a police officer in Sarajevo. He joined the police force in 1984, and by 1992 was a criminal inspector investigating serious crimes such as homicide. He gave further evidence as follows: During the war, the police continued to operate. If the Bosnian army, the ABiH, was unable to repel an attack, it would call upon certain police services, including members of special police forces, for assistance. On some occasions, regular police were also called upon to assist. During the war, municipal police investigated incidents where persons were wounded while the witness and 20 fellow criminal inspectors investigated sniping and shelling incidents involving fatalities. The witness operated in a civilian area, and accordingly the victims of the incidents he investigated were by and large civilians. He investigated over 100 incidents where civilians were killed. He did not recall one day through the war when there was not some form of attack on the city. Mr. Kucanin gave evidence about a number of specific incidents he investigated or attended, including one involving a nine-year-old boy who was shot and wounded on the 22nd of July 1994, and another involving a two-year-old girl who was shot and killed on the 28th of July, 1993. He also gave evidence about two shelling incidents which occurred on the 9th of November 1993. On the afternoon of that date, the witness attended the scene in Alipasino Polje, a district in the western area of Sarajevo where the incident occurred. At this juncture, I would ask the witness to take the pointer on the desk to his right and point to Alipasino Polje on the map. Perhaps we might have an image of the map on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, could you please point to the area of Alipasino Polje. I should indicate for the record that the map the witness is pointing to is tab 12 of Exhibit 586.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is pointing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On my screen, Your Honour, the picture lacks any significant detail. I don't know whether we could improve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, tab 12 being a previous number P3658, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. A mortar shell which was assessed to be 120 millimetres impacted alongside a gap between two concrete barriers which protected a makeshift schoolroom in a residential block of apartments. Four persons were killed, being the teacher and three children, and 21 were injured, being mostly children. On the same day following that incident, another 120-millimetre shell, mortar shell, impacted some 200 metres away on Rade Koncara Square in Alipasino Polje. There was a personnel department of the Kulin Ban unit nearby. Mostly women work there. Three civilians were killed and approximately 18 injured. Later, several others died of their injuries. An investigation which included a ballistics expert established the direction of fire for both shells to have been from Nedzarici, part of which was in Bosnian Serb army control. It was mandatory for each investigation team to include a ballistics expert, which meant that often the witness and his fellow investigators were able to determine the likely source of fire. Many of these sources became notorious. There was no variation in these sources of fire throughout the war. Mr. Kucanin marked a map which is tab 12, Exhibit 586, with the sites of sources of Bosnian Serb army fire. He gave evidence that these sites were determined from investigations either led by him or in which he was a participating member. Between September 1992 and August 1994, he conducted about 20 investigations as the lead investigator and participated in about 20 others. The areas marked by Mr. Kucanin in relation to the sources of shelling fire, firstly, are as follows: The area of the village of Mrkovici was marked with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, could you please point to the letter A on the map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the camera could zoom in so we could see that letter on the map. Again, Your Honours, I have no detail on my screen. I don't know whether the contrast could be adjusted. The area of Mrkovici was a source of shelling of the upper part of Sarajevo in the Stari Grad and Centar municipalities. The witness said that he participated in a team which investigated the Markale shelling incident in February 1994, and he believed the shell came from that area. Letter B refers to Burije, which does not quite appear on the map but in the direction to the east of the city, that is to the right. Could you please point to the letter B. This was a source of heavy artillery. And as I invite the witness to point to these places, perhaps the camera could zoom in on that part of the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point to the letter B again, and could we please see that part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Trebevic mountain, position C. Could you please point to that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had several positions from which the upper parts of the city were targeted. The old part of the town was targeted from this position. The next position is D, Zlastiste, on the south-western side of Trebevic mountain. There was a barracks in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Source of shelling against Sarajevo. Miljevic, position D1. Please point to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a notorious source of fire and there was artillery placed in that position. Vraca, position E, is just above Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Source of mortar and artillery fire. The centre of Sarajevo was exposed to that position. Position F, Gavrica Brdo. The witness was unable to be precise about the location of the hill and marked its approximate position with the letter F. Please point to the letter F. It was the source of artillery fire into Dobrinja. Please point to Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Meljine, position G, was the position of a church of the Orthodox faith from which Dobrinja was targeted by mortars. Perhaps we could see that again with the camera zooming in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also please point to Lukavica whilst you are in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we see that position? Thank you. All right. Nedzarici, position H. Bosnian Serb military barracks were located here from which Alipasino Polje and Alipasino Most were shelled. Would you point again to H.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you point again to Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you now please point to Alipasin Most.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The forestry school, position I, was a source of -- if we could see that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a source of artillery and mortar fire against Bosnian-held parts of Ilidza and Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica and the Igman road. If you point to the area of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we see that, please. Thank you. Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: This is the Sokolovic colony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates] .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Igman road.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Roughly here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next position, position J, Paljevo, from which there was shelling of the entire lower part of the town, including the Rajlovac area and Buca Potok. Please point to the Rajlovac area.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Position K, Krivoglavci near Vogosca, a source of mortar fire against parts of Vogosca. Please point to position L, will you please point to position L. Blagovac. Could we see that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was a source of tank and mortar fire onto Bosnian parts of Vogosca. Please point to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: These parts here also belong to Vogosca municipality and they were also exposed to shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Position L.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Position M, Polinje, please point to that. Was a wide area of many places from where the centre of Sarajevo was targeted with artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kromolj, position N. Please point to that. Was an area which was a source of artillery fire against the Kosevo stadium and the neighbourhoods of - and perhaps you could point to these areas - Bare -- Do you see Bare on the map? Please point to it. Braca. Thank you. And the road which links those neighbourhoods to the city.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Lukavica barracks, position O, you've already indicated, had heavy artillery which impacted on the lower parts of the town, meaning from the Marsal Tito barracks downwards, including the municipalities of Novo Sarajevo and Novi Grad. Position P, the Rajlovac barracks, and you've already pointed to the area of Rajlovac, was a source of fire against Sokolac -- could you please point to Sokolac -- and the railroad tracks --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Correction: Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness also indicated sources of sniping fire, the first of those being, number 1, Spicasta Stijena. Could you please point to number 1, the area of Spicasta Stijena, Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we see that, please. A notorious source of sniper fire resulting in many such casualties. Villages around were sniped and the older part of the city. Number 2, Osmice. The witness gave evidence that the city was fired upon by weapons known as death sowers and snipers, the largest amount of such firing coming from here and Vraca. Would you please explain what a death sower was, that is the weapon known colloquially as a death sower.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: It's a name used because it fires quickly, but it is an automatic light machine-gun which came to be known as the death sower. It's a machine-gun with supports. In the army of Yugoslavia, these had optical vision, optical sites, so they were used to identify targets, and they were inherited by the Serbian army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness also identified some areas above Grbavica being the Jewish cemetery, indicated with the number 3. Would you firstly point to the number 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you indicate more specifically where the actual cemetery was or is. Could you point to the cemetery itself.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness indicates a whitish portion of the map immediately to the right of the number 4. Thank you. And Gornji Kovacici. Please point to that, position number 4. I think you've already done that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vraca region up to the police school, number 5. Please point to number 5.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area from the Vrbanja bridge to the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge, including four skyscrapers in Lenjinova street, all of about 15 storeys, indicated by a line and number 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also three skyscrapers referred to as the shopping centre at Grbavica targeted the centre of the town and Titova street, accounting for the killing of a large number of civilians. This source more or less formed a triangle and is indicated by a triangle with the number 4. Could you please point to that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness marked an intersection with a cross and number 5 and a circle where a number of civilians were killed by fire from these three skyscrapers at the intersection of Marsal Tito and Djure Djakovica street. Would you please point to that circle with the cross and number 5.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness worked on three investigations involving trams that were hit from this area. The position of those trams when hit were marked with crosses and the numbers 6, 7, and 8. Would you point to those.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness also marked a building, Metalka, with a cross and number 2. Would you please point to that. And was a source that of fire or a place where fire was received?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates] It was a source of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness also gave evidence that a particular dangerous street for civilians was called Tracanska street. Would you please point to that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Tracanska. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And while you're locating it, the witness gave evidence that the area was dangerous all the way to the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge. Would you please indicate that area.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence was given that dozens of civilians were killed here. Number 6, Osrenska street. Please indicate the general position of Osrenska street. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Source of fire. Zagorska street, number 7. Please point to that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness gave evidence that this was determined to be the source of fire for the incident involving the wounding of a nine-year-old boy. It was determined by lining up two impact points made by one of the bullets fired during that incident. Milinkladska street, number 8.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the witness marked areas where received fire from these three streets with blue lines circled with a capital Z. Please point to that part of the city on the map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see to the north of that position.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just in terms of the geography, how do the positions of those three streets compare in terms of altitude to the area marked with the letter Z? Are those streets higher, on the same altitude, or lower?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: It's a hill on that part of Sarajevo where those streets are, and there are many small streets there parallel with the streets in town and vertical to the streets in town. In any event, it's a hill at a higher altitude than the rest of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please now point to position 9, Miroslava Krleze, a street in Dobrinja from which fire was received in the Bosnian-held parts of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Nedzarici you've already indicated, bears the number 10, was especially hazardous, including from the witness's own experience when travelling down Lukavica Cesta and Ante Babica. Could you point to those two streets, approximately, on the map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed the witness marked four streets with a circle and capital Y where frequently sniping -- persons were shot from sniping. Rajlovac barracks, again number 11.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness heard from other investigators that fire was received in Sokolje from this source. And finally, position 12, Kromolj. Could you please point to that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which fire was received in northern parts of the city. Mr. Kucanin, did these sources of fire according to investigations which you either led or in which you partook apply throughout the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, from the very beginning of the war until the end. It was from these places that fire was most frequently opened against Sarajevo, though there were other places too, but according to my experience and that of my colleagues, these were the most active in opening fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kucanin, on page 2 of your statement from the 4th of September 2000, in paragraphs 4 and 5, you stated that in the zone of the police of the city of Sarajevo before the war, there were ten police stations, out of which four after the war remained under the control of the BH government, as you say, whereas the others were taken over by the Serbian police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Sarajevo police force broke up into a section under the control of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and under the control of the Serb authorities at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: This was a forcible takeover of police stations by the army. The police force, the Serb police forces, of course, and the reservists of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The police stations in municipalities Centar, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, and Stari Grad remained under the control of the Bosnian authorities. Those are the four central municipalities of Sarajevo, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Pale police stations were in Pale, Ilidza, Trnovo, Hadzici, Ilijas, and Vogosca. They are on the periphery, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so, though Ilijas and Vogosca are closer to town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any event, they're peripheral in relation to these central municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Mr. Kucanin, that before the war it was in the peripheral areas of Sarajevo and the villages around it that were inhabited by Serbs whereas the Muslim population was mostly concentrated in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite agree though I don't know. I know that in Ilijas there were Serbs and Muslims. It maybe sounds strange but there were maybe just a hundred or so more Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But this division of police stations into those under Serb control and those under government control, did that more or less correspond to that distribution of the population in the territory of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I said a moment ago there was forcible takeover of police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the way in which this happened, I'm just asking whether the police stations corresponded more or less to the majority population.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I said a moment ago about Ilijas. The same applies to Vogosca. The population there was not dominated by Serbs. In Hadzici, again more or less; in Trnovo too. But I pointed out that parts of the city of Sarajevo were captured by the Serb army, even as far as Grbavica, which need not mean that their aim was to divide it up according to ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the aim or the method. I am talking about the factual situation. Did it reflect the factual situation roughly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer with any certainty. I'd be glad to. I know about Ilijas for certain because I lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. And paragraph 2 of the same statement - I am talking of the same one because you gave three statements, so I have to mention that - you were talking about the stations under Muslim control. There were about a hundred or so policemen left to man all four police stations, which is rather a small number. Does it mean that in those stations there was some Serb policemen and that they had left them and joined the Serb police and army? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Croats and Muslims also abandon police stations?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't, because I came to work on that day when everything blew up. There were quite a number of Serbs still in the stations. All the Muslims came to work. Some Croats did not report to work. They were in town, but with the consolidation of the police force, they returned. However, the police who wanted to immediately left to go to Ilijas, Pale, depending on where they were assigned to go to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement from 1995, speaking about the sources of shelling, and I quote you, this is page 01039347, paragraphs 4 and 5: "When those places are marked on the map, you will see that Sarajevo was completely surrounded by positions held by the Bosnian Serb army from which the town was shelled. The Bosnian Serb army could easily select targets in town because they knew the town and many of them had lived in the town before the war." That is what you said; isn't that right? So it follows from your statement that a considerable number of members of units of the army of Republika Srpska who were around Sarajevo came from the town of Sarajevo itself. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a large number left Sarajevo and joined the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they came from the town of Sarajevo itself; right? Please answer with words, because a nod does not enter into the record. You know that as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why did they leave their homes in town and went up to the surrounding mountains?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: In my judgement, the SDS issued a proclamation to the Serb people to leave the town of Sarajevo because they had planned in a blitzkrieg, that is with rapid intervention, to take control of the main features in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So they left upon instructions from the SDS, for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, maybe a small number left out of fear, but most left in order to come back as victors to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, those who left out of fear, what were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: The war, just as I was afraid of it, and everyone. We didn't know what lay in wait for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on in that same statement on the same page, you say in paragraph 7 that many members of the army of Republika Srpska before the war used to work in the Geodesi Institute [phoen] and took maps from there. The same applies to the faculty of architecture. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it clear that around Sarajevo, in units of the army of Republika Srpska, there were inhabitants of Sarajevo itself and the surroundings who had fled to the hills?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, together with members of the Yugoslav People's Army who dug in there two months before the war started in Sarajevo, who brought the weapons, the artillery, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about the whole period of the war, not just the period of the existence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the question is: You say that many left and went up into the hills. Many had worked in various institutions and left. So the units of the army of Republika Srpska which I'm referring to consisted of inhabitants of the surrounding villages and suburbs and inhabitants of the city centre itself who went there, some that were called to go, some out of fear, or some for some other reasons that only you can guess about.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, you know that. But you know that the Yugoslav army was in the city of Sarajevo and around it until the 16th or 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how the Yugoslav People's Army left Sarajevo, how it pulled out, you know that better than me, what the circumstances of that were, but you're not testifying about that and that's why I'm not asking you about that. What I am asking you is this: If we have observed this, then what kind of aggression could it have been? What aggression are you talking about if that was the case? For example, the page 3370139337, the last paragraph there, and you say the aggressor -- you use the term "aggressor positions." And on page 344, you talk about the "aggressor side" and so on and so forth. Those are the terms you use. So when you talk about aggression and occupation in your 1995 statement, for example, you say territories occupied by the army of Bosnian Serbs. Isn't it clear that in the town of Sarajevo, along the lines that separated the parts with the majority Muslim population and the Serb population, the periphery and surrounding villages, that that's where the front line was formed, and on both sides people were from the locality? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. Milosevic. I've already told you. Many villages were inhabited by Muslims. Take part of Ilijas once again, the upper part of Ilijas, and Vogosca. So I cannot agree that it was -- that the defence line was formed along ethnic lines. And let me answer your first point and observation, the one you made. How come Ratko Mladic came to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where was he from? And Milutin Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, as far as I know, Ratko Mladic was from the environs of Sarajevo himself, just like yourself. He wasn't born either in Serbia or in some other republic. He was born in the environs of Sarajevo, and he went to the JNA, and he was there until the army of Republika Srpska was formed, just like your General Delic used to be in the JNA and that other man, the commander of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Budakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Budakovic. He was in the JNA too, just like Naser Oric was in the JNA or the police or whatever, and just like many other officers of yours. Sefer Halilovic, a case in point, who was the first commander. He was also in the JNA. And in that they differ from Ratko Mladic who was born in Trnovo, for example, several kilometres away from Sarajevo. Sefer Halilovic, on the other hand, was born in Pripolje, in Serbia, and he never did service in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. You can give evidence in due course if you wish, but you're not giving it now. Now, you're supposed to be asking this witness questions. What is the question you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last two paragraphs on that same side, you say that the command of the army of Bosnian Serbs gave the Serbs who worked in those institutions before the war, that is to say the Garavetski Sabor [phoen], the land surveying office, to leave town and take the maps with them. And I'm quoting you: "This is evidence that before the war started, the Bosnian Serbs wanted to encircle the town and have all information for shelling the city at their disposal." How do you know about these instructions by the command of the Bosnian Serb army, as you call it? People working in those institutions probably did have maps. You had maps yourself. They had maps. You were all inhabitants of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I want to make one thing clear to you: Many people stayed on in Sarajevo. Many Serbs remained in Sarajevo, in actual fact. So the information that I set forward wasn't difficult to come by, and in fact, we came across empty spaces there where the maps used to be stored. And many people came to us and owned up. And I was perhaps the most objective policeman in town, or at least one of the most objective ones. My wife was born in Belgrade - perhaps I shouldn't say that but she was - and I am very objective, I really am. And whenever I talk to those Serbs and told them that they could come to me for protection, they would tell me about things like that themselves. Many remained. They didn't have anywhere to go. They had always lived there. They handed over their weapons to us because the SDS people had armed them, so they handed over their weapons and handed over various lists of the units that had been formed and the people and what they were in charge of. And I even got information about a man that was supposed to kill me from a colleague. I took refuge and went to another service. So things like that weren't difficult to come by, information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kucanin. You say the Serbs remained in Sarajevo. Well, I assume you know that nobody could leave Sarajevo, in actual fact, that it was prohibited. Nobody was allowed to leave. Your authorities didn't let people leave. And as you're testifying about sniper fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness deal with that before you go on to something else. The accused is suggesting that the authorities in Sarajevo did not allow people to leave. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you this: I wanted to send my wife to Belgrade at the time. However, she cried and said she didn't want to go. But Yugoslav air force planes, transport planes and other JAT planes would fly over the airport and land and leave, and the Yugoslav People's Army held the airport under its control. It had assumed control of the airport, and it was only those planes that would take off and land. And then the bulk of the population of Sarajevo or, rather, the Serb inhabitants left in the direction of Belgrade and other parts of Serbia. Some Muslims, Muslim inhabitants left too because people in the beginning believed in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. I did too. But when I saw that things had come to a head, then the Muslims did not any more and did not take that direction any more. Whereas the authorities hadn't been established yet and there was no consolidated authority. So nobody actually prevented those people from leaving Sarajevo. Transport planes flew in during the night and people crossed over from Grbavica, and I saw with my very own eyes the Yugoslav flag flying on those transporters. So people would go to the airport and from the airport they were taken off elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, that was at the beginning when the JNA was withdrawing and when family members were being transported of the JNA servicemen. I'm talking about the war, the time you're testifying about. So after what period of time were people not allowed to leave Sarajevo pursuant to a decision taken by the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know about a decision of that kind. I know that all military-able men were not supposed to leave. We needed permission to do so. But to leave Sarajevo otherwise under a siege and encirclement as you can see on the map behind me was impossible. To pass across the two lines without being fired at was impossible. Later on, various convoys were organised by international organisations. People left in buses and coaches and did what they could, but that was under escort by international forces. That was how they managed to leave. But to leave Sarajevo otherwise was just not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that there was a ban for citizens to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I've already told you, I don't know about a ban of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say you don't know. Fine. Now, what you say in your statement about the division of the police stations and the participants of Serbs -- citizens of Sarajevo in the fighting around town - I'm taking all this from your own statement - does that not speak of the fact that it wasn't the Serbs who surrounded the town but took up the positions in localities where they lived and where they happened to find themselves when they were objectively forced out of the centre of town? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Well, it is partially correct, but I can't confirm something when there is a bit of both. A bit of both is true. And a moment ago when I was talking about the division, I forgot to say that the Novo Sarajevo police station, for instance, on this map - if I may I'll point it to you, its locality - and Novi Grad, the police station, was in the centre of Sarajevo, and we fought for three nights with the army and the Serb police to prevent them taking control of those two police stations as well because they were supposed to be taken over. So there wasn't any ethnic division that coincided with the separation line, but Novo Sarajevo and Novi Grad is in the centre of town and there were quite a lot of attempts to save people. You know the radio and television station. I'm sure you know where that is. On several occasions, those towers -- attempts were made to take over the towers and the television station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that now, neither did you talk about it in these statements of yours. And because my time is limited, I shall restrict myself to your statements. You claim, therefore, that there was no ban on leaving town.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No. I said I didn't know about a decision of that kind. I didn't know about a ban. I wasn't a high-ranking functionary myself or somebody which necessarily must have known about that. All I do know is when a state of emergency was proclaimed and mobilisation, that is to say that the people had to defend the town with the weapons they had and all people of age, over the age of 19 or whatever, up to the age of 55, had to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But do you know -- and if you don't, let me tell you that the authorities in Sarajevo banned citizens from leaving town. Do you know that the Serb forces around Sarajevo didn't prevent anybody from leaving and crossing across their territory, passing through their territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serb forces, for example, shot at buses, evacuating children, small children, and that a two-month-old baby was killed during an incident like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a tragic event. I don't know about it but I can assume there were such cases as well. However, my question for you was do you know that the army of Republika Srpska did not prevent any civilians from leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Yes, it did. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you. You can give a no answer and we can move on. From your statement, Mr. Kucanin, we could conclude that the Muslim side saw the war completely unarmed and unprepared, saw the advent of the war.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. According to the documents I have, that was not so. My question to you is as follows: Do you know that the Party of Democratic Action of Alija Izetbegovic, as early on as the spring, had the military wing of the party, which was called the Patriotic League? Have you heard about that organisation? Did you have any information about it? Have you heard about the formations and units of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I'm not a member of the party. I have heard of the Patriotic League. And when you sum everything up, I'm sorry that I wasn't a member of the Patriotic League, because it was the first to organise itself, along with the police force, to defend the country. And as to its organisation, I can't speak about that because I wasn't a member myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm sure you know that it was set up on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that day is celebrated as the Patriotic League day over there.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: As I say, I wasn't a member of the league myself and I can't see that from the media. I don't know that that day is celebrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is how it is being celebrated, for those who are interested - perhaps you're not interested in it - which, of course, is a positive side of you as an individual, but I did assume you knew about it. But if not, let's move on. As you live in Sarajevo; is that right? Did you have a chance of seeing in January 1999 or reading in the Sarajevo paper Oslobodjenje a series of Sefko Hodzic entitled "The Secrets of the Patriotic League"? And it speaks about the inception of the organisation, the paramilitary organisation at that time and its structure and establishment.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I'd be happy to answer your question, but I really didn't read those articles or series of articles. I don't read the Oslobodjenje, I read other newspapers that I like more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you don't know that the day is officially celebrated, that is to say the 31st of March, as Patriotic League day. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, as you're a policeman, do you know that Hasan Brkic street - he was also a Muslim and he was a partisan dating back to the days of the national liberation war - and it is a big Sarajevo street, and it has been renamed and is now called Patriotic League street. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that in the amendments to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina enacted in the summer of 1990 there was a ban, in addition to other things, political organisation and work jeopardising the territorial integrity of the SFRY. That was in conformity and pursuant to the Yugoslav constitution. And I assume in view of the work you did before the war that you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I can't say that I am with any certainty, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Any answer I could give you might not be the right one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you about that then, although there is a lot of proof and evidence illustrating that. But let me move on and ask some other witness about that kind of organisation who might be able to tell us more about it. Do you happen to know that from April to September 1991, from Sarajevo, three or four times groups of 15 to 20 men were sent for training as terrorists to some Arab countries. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Green Berets? Have you heard of them? And they were led by Emin Surakic, and the volunteer units of the Mujahedin, specialists for the rear and other units of military organisation in Bosnia under the leadership of Kerim Ricarevic and others, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I have heard of the Green Berets. Now, the rest of your information wasn't correct. They were -- the Green Berets were called Bosnae, and that was a historical title of -- and what Bosnia was called at one time in its history. So I did hear of them. They were all patriotic forces that were setting up resistance in an effort to save the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "patriotic forces," you yourself were a policeman. I assume you know that Jusuf Juka Prazina, for example, was a criminal before the war and he commanded some of those forces, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he a criminal?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Ramiz Delalic? Was he a criminal too?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who else except for Juka Prazina of the infamous criminals formed some units around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Infamous, I don't know that any infamous ones were formed. Juka, and his name is Prazina, we knew of his past history and we placed him under police command precisely because we had heard some ugly things about him, ugly stories about him taking in Serbs for interrogation by people who weren't competent to do so. So that unit together with Juka Prazina was placed under the supervision and surveillance of police forces, and they received accreditation, and Kerim Ricarevic was their commander. So from that time on they were not able to work independently or autonomously. Later on, the unit disintegrated, and you know how Juka Prazina ended up. He ended the way -- his life the way he had lived his life. But I and my colleagues personally spent some time in that unit. Actually, we spent days there to prevent any crimes from being perpetrated by its members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you consider that the activities of those armed formations such as the one that Juka Prazina commanded and similar ones were in fact -- gave rise to reasonable fear that the Serbs felt, the civilian population which was leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Juka Prazina didn't form his unit before the war, as far as I know. It was only once the war had begun, as one of the more courageous men, rallied a group around him. He always wanted to be a leader, and he formed his group, and that is how it started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But do you know as a policeman, and you are one of the few who is testifying under his full name rather than as a protected witness in this case, that in May and June 1991 in Sarajevo, that is May and June 1991, which is almost a year prior to the outbreak of the war, a Green Beret unit who was still in civilian clothes at the time were training in handling weapons in the cinema hall in the streets of Dragica Pravica in the evening, in the Bistrik hall. Did you fail to notice these activities?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I truly didn't know about them. I do know that once in the region that you mentioned they stopped a military vehicle of the JNA. I remember the banana affair because it contained rockets and on the loading documents it said bananas. And this vehicle was stopped by members of those Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that when joining the Patriotic League members took an oath to the Muslim people? This was a party army which in a multinational environment rallied members of a single nation.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me go on to things that I'm certain you do know about, and I'll go back to your statement. In paragraph 1 on page 3 -- 01131 -- the statement of 2005 [as interpreted], you say at the end of 1992 -- you say the end of 1992, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed. The Ministry of the Interior was required for the needs of defence to attach to the army the reserve police force. It is well known that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formally formed on the 15th of April, 1992, and that is Army Day in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: It is true that that day is being celebrated but that was not when the army was formed. I know exactly when it was formed. It was in the autumn of 1992. Up until then these were just units that may have been called various names but they all had one name in mind to defend the town of Sarajevo. But in 1992, I know, because our police reservists went to join the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kucanin. So even the fact that Army Day is being celebrated on the 15th of April, as you know --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- doesn't seem to indicate that that is the formal date when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 on page 3 of your statement of 2000, you said that the Serbs targeted especially religious buildings, especially with artillery, mortars, and heavy weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that they especially targeted, but they did target religious buildings all the time, but not in particular. If I were to say in particular, if I were to say how many civilians were killed in the city of Sarajevo, it would appear that they had specially targeted civilians. But they did target religious buildings, and I did investigate those cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
